title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the quotation to the final draft

questions.prompt: Leila told her father: "I have lost my keys in your car." Which sentence reports her words?

options.text: Leila told to her father that she had lost her keys in his car.
Leila said her father that she had lost her keys in his car.
Leila told her father that she had lost her keys in his car.
Leila told her father that she had lost my keys in your car.

questions.explanation: Three things move at once. The tense steps back: the present perfect have lost becomes the past perfect had lost. The pronouns move to the reporter's point of view: Leila's I becomes she, her my becomes her, and the your that pointed at her father becomes his — leaving my keys and your car keeps the reader inside Leila's mouth. And the reporting verb has to be the right one: you tell somebody something, but you say something to somebody, so "said her father" and "told to her father" both mix the two patterns.

questions.prompt: You are writing your first draft, the stage where notes become sentences. Your notes are: "Teachers – special training – identify – learning difficulties – early." Which sentence develops them?

options.text: Teachers need special training to identify learning difficulties early.
Teachers special training identify learning difficulties early.
Teachers needing special training to identify learning difficulties early.
Teachers are needed special training to identify learning difficulties early.

questions.explanation: Developing notes means putting back everything telegraphic notes leave out: a finite verb, the small grammar words, and the link between the two ideas. "Teachers need special training to identify learning difficulties early." has a finite verb, need, and an infinitive of purpose, to identify, which says what the training is for. Copying the notes with the dashes removed is still a list; the version built on needing has no finite verb and cannot stand alone; and the passive version turns the teachers into the thing that is needed, which is not what the notes say.

questions.prompt: Match each symbol of the correction code with the mistake it points to in your draft.

options.text: V
P
C
a comma or a full stop used where it should not be
a word that does not exist, or one that does not fit the meaning
a small letter at the beginning of a proper noun
a word left out of the sentence

questions.explanation: V stands for Vocabulary — a word that does not exist or that has been misused. P stands for Punctuation — the wrong mark, or a mark in the wrong place. C stands for Capitalization — a capital letter missing or wrongly used, as at the start of a proper noun. And the tick means that something has simply been left out of the sentence. The other symbols of the code are G for a grammar mistake, S for a spelling mistake, W.L for a wrong linker and W.O. for a wrong word order.

questions.prompt: Read this note from a school magazine: "Our library now opens at seven in the morning. Many pupils travel in from the villages and reach school long before the first lesson. ___, the number of readers before eight o'clock has tripled since September." Which link word fits the blank?

options.text: However
Therefore
Although
Otherwise

questions.explanation: The two sentences before the blank give a cause — the library opens early and the pupils arrive early — and the sentence after it gives the result of that cause, so the blank calls for a linker of consequence: Therefore. "However" would announce a contrast, but the three readings all point the same way; "Although" opens a subordinate clause and cannot stand alone before a comma; and "Otherwise" would mean "if the library did not open early", which is exactly the opposite of what the note has just said.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Integrating pupils with special needs ___ trained staff, suitable equipment and the support of every parent."

options.text: acquires
requests
requires
inquires

questions.explanation: "Require" means to need something as a necessary condition, which is exactly what the sentence says about integration. "Acquire" means to obtain or gain something, as in to acquire a second language; "request" means to ask for something politely, as in to request a meeting; and "inquire" means to ask for information, as in to inquire about the timetable. The four verbs are confused for one reason only: they look alike.

questions.prompt: Your classmate has handed your draft back with several symbols of the correction code in the margin. According to the writing process, what do you do next?

options.text: You pass the draft to a second classmate for another review.
You copy the draft out neatly and hand it in to the teacher.
You go back to step one and generate new ideas for the article.
You revise the draft and make the changes.

questions.explanation: Sharing and responding is followed by revising and editing: the symbols in the margin exist to be acted on, and revising is where the changes are made. Copying out a draft you have not corrected preserves every mistake it contains; going back to generating ideas throws away a plan that is already built; and a second review only postpones the work. The final neat draft comes last, once nothing is left to change.
